sentences.text: Fossils of this pterosaur reveal jaws that lack teeth and feature low, protruding rims without a crest.
The defining holotype specimen consists merely of a snout fragment measuring approximately five centimeters in length.
Harry Govier Seeley initially placed three toothless snout fragments from the Lower Cretaceous Cambridge Greensand of England into the genus Ornithocheirus in 1869.
He then provisionally named these fragments a separate genus called Ornithostoma, a name derived from Greek words for "bird" and "mouth".
Seeley formally established the genus in 1871 for fragmented bone remains, mostly jaws, of a toothless pterosaur from the Upper Cretaceous of England.
In 1891, Seeley formally named the type species Ornithostoma sedgwicki and referred pelvis elements to it, claiming they were identical to Pteranodon.
The Paleobiology Database lists the parent group of Ornithostoma as Azhdarchoidea.
The time range for Ornithostoma is estimated from 106.3 to 100.5 million years ago during the Albian stage.
S. Christopher Bennett considered Ornithostoma distinct from Pteranodon due to jaw ridges but concluded it was a nomen dubium in 1994.
David Unwin rejected the nomen dubium status in 2001, arguing Ornithostoma is a valid genus in Pteranodontidae with a wingspan of 2-3 meters based on limited material.
In 2012, Alexander O. Averianov suggested Ornithostoma belongs to Azhdarchoidea based on a combination of jaw and postcranial traits.
Subsequent studies suggest Ornithostoma is a member of the family Chaoyangopteridae.
In 1994, S. Christopher Bennett noted that Ornithostoma has been treated as a wastebasket taxon for remains lacking distinctive features, similar to the dinosaur Megalosaurus.
